name: Generation effect
statement: A word a learner produces from a cue and a rule is remembered better than the same word read off the page.
meaning: The paradigm holds the words constant and varies only how they arrive. A learner sees rapid-fast and reads it, or sees rapid-f under the rule synonym and says fast. The same item serves both conditions across learners, so nothing about word choice can explain the difference. Two features separate this from the testing effect, which the atlas treats as a neighbouring entry. Generation is a manipulation of encoding, not of practice after encoding, and the item being produced comes out of semantic memory rather than out of the study episode. Slamecka and Graf raised that second point themselves, noting that generating might be an instance of recall with semantic memory as the source, and that such an account risks restating the finding rather than explaining it. The effect is measured against reading, and reading is a weak comparison. Nothing in the paradigm compares generating against a learner's own best alternative strategy.

origin.who: Norman J. Slamecka and Peter Graf
origin.where: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning and Memory
origin.note: The paper is "The generation effect: Delineation of a phenomenon", and it names the effect. Slamecka and Graf described their own purpose as empirical rather than theoretical, writing that a search of the journals had uncovered no thoroughgoing treatment of the question and no cumulative body of literature. Their closing position was that the effect is real and poses an interpretative problem, and they declined to choose among the four explanations they had raised.

evidence: Slamecka and Graf ran five experiments on University of Toronto undergraduates. Experiment 1 used 24 subjects and a 100-item list, 20 items under each of five rules: associate (lamp-light), category (ruby-diamond), opposite (long-short), synonym (sea-ocean) and rhyme (save-cave). Generation errors ran at a median 6%, and those items were dropped from scoring. Generated words were recognised more often, F(1, 20) = 9.68, MSe = .07, and were rated with higher confidence, F(1, 20) = 6.92, MSe = 1.04. Pacing did nothing: timed and self-paced means of .75 and .79, F < 1. Rules mattered for overall level, F(4, 80) = 5.28, because rhyme responses sat lowest, but rules did not interact with generating, F(4, 80) = 2.09. Experiment 2 moved the contrast inside the subject, 12 people seeing both conditions, and the effect held at F(1, 10) = 27.17, MSe = .04. Warning subjects about the test changed nothing, with informed and uninformed means of .72 and .77, F < 1. Asked to label each recognised word as generated or read, subjects were right 74% of the time against a chance value of 50%, t(11) = 6.00, SE = .04. Experiment 3 asked whether the benefit spreads to the cue. Twenty-four subjects saw 66 rhyme pairs and were tested on either the stimulus or the response side, with the untested member always supplied. Generating helped responses, t(20) = 5.94, and did nothing for stimuli, t < 1, giving an interaction of F(1, 20) = 10.75, MSe = 50.99. Experiment 4 put 12 subjects through five cycles of study and free recall of 60 responses. Generated words won, F(1, 11) = 19.84, MSe = .05, and the two curves converged over the last two trials, F(4, 44) = 4.47. Output position ruled out one artefact: generated items were not recalled earlier, with mean output positions of 13.45 against 12.74 across all trials. Experiment 5 ran 24 subjects through five cycles of cued recall on the 66 rhyme pairs. Response recall was .68 generated against .61 read, and stimulus recall was .53 against .51, F(1, 22) = 6.19, MSe = .02. The response-side selectivity found in Experiment 3 did not reach significance here, F(1, 22) = 1.82. Condition means for the recognition experiments are printed in figures rather than in the text, so no recognition proportions are quoted from this paper.

replication.headline: McCurdy and colleagues pooled 1,653 estimates from 310 experiments and found generated items remembered .102 more often than read items, 95% CI [.087, .117].
replication.detail: Two meta-analyses reach the same place by different routes. Bertsch, Pesta, Wiscott and McDaniel searched PsycINFO from 1966 to 2005, asked primary researchers for file-drawer studies, and pooled 445 effect sizes from 86 studies covering 17,711 subjects. Weighted mean proportions were .471 read against .559 generated, an advantage of .088, which they standardised against the read condition to give .40, 95% CI [.38, .42]. Letting each experiment contribute a single mean moved that to .41, 95% CI [.39, .43]. Sampling error accounted for 11% of the observed variance, so the pooled figure hides real differences between conditions. McCurdy, Viechtbauer, Sklenar, Frankenstein and Leshikar covered 126 articles, 310 experiments and 1,653 estimates, and reported the raw difference rather than a standardised one: .102, 95% CI [.087, .117]. Their moderators track Bertsch's. Recognition gave .144, 95% CI [.121, .167], cued recall .132, 95% CI [.076, .189], and free recall .095, 95% CI [.042, .148]. Within-subjects designs gave .144, 95% CI [.126, .161], t(119) = 16.24, p < .001, against .073, 95% CI [.031, .114] between subjects. The pure-list figure is the one that settles an old argument. Bertsch and colleagues describe Slamecka and Katsaiti's proposal that the effect is an artefact of learners abandoning rehearsal of read items in mixed lists, which predicts nothing in a pure list. McCurdy and colleagues found .103, 95% CI [.071, .149] for pure lists against .144, 95% CI [.125, .162] for mixed. Correcting for small-study effects by extrapolating to infinite sample size cut the overall estimate to .080, 95% CI [.048, .111], which still excludes zero.

study.cite: McCurdy, M. P., Viechtbauer, W., Sklenar, A. M., Frankenstein, A. N., & Leshikar, E. D. (2020). Theories of the generation effect and the impact of generation constraint: A meta-analytic review. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 27(6), 1139-1165.

limits: The effect has boundaries the pooled figures bury. In Bertsch and colleagues' table, nonword stimuli gave .05, 95% CI [.03, .07], against .41 for words and .87 for numbers. Anagrams reversed it, -.05, 95% CI [-.07, -.03], across 18 studies and more than 1,000 subjects. Lists longer than 50 items gave .09, 95% CI [.07, .11], against .60 for lists of 25 or fewer. Two of their intervals deserve caution. Nearly every confidence interval in that table is the estimate plus or minus .02, whether the row rests on 15 effect sizes or 445. One row prints an effect size of .37 beside an interval of .49 to .53, which does not contain it. Schmidt and Cherry ran four between-list experiments and found generation hurting free recall of word pairs, cued recall of the second word, pair integration and clustering, while helping recognition and free recall of second words alone. Their reading is that generation buys item processing at the cost of processing relations. The educational case is the weakest part. Schindler and Richter pooled 129 effect sizes from 20 studies, nested in 74 samples and 3,551 participants, for a text generation effect of g = 0.41, 95% CI [0.31, 0.52], with heavy heterogeneity, Q(128) = 528.26, p < .001. Within that, texts over 900 words gave g = 0.05 and sentence unscrambling of expository texts gave g = 0.77. The same authors then tried to reproduce the second figure. Across seven experiments varying intentionality, time limits, retention interval and design, with samples from 40 to 152 and materials of 12 six-sentence texts from a psychology textbook chapter on Bandura, they found no positive generation effect on prompted recall anywhere. Four experiments favoured reading: Experiment 3, OR = 0.69, 95% CI [0.53, 0.90]; Experiment 4, OR = 0.80, 95% CI [0.64, 1.00]; Experiment 5, OR = 0.80, 95% CI [0.70, 0.91]; Experiment 7, OR = 0.76, 95% CI [0.65, 0.89]. One multiple-choice result in Experiment 6 went the other way, OR = 1.18, 95% CI [1.01, 1.38]. Their conclusion is that applications of text generation in education are rather limited. Sources searched were Crossref, Unpaywall, PubMed Central, and the full texts of Slamecka and Graf, Bertsch and colleagues, McCurdy and colleagues, Schindler and Richter's meta-analysis and their 2025 replication series. No multi-site or many-labs replication of the word-level effect was located, and no body of work on what learners believe about generating, comparable to the metacognitive half of the testing effect, was located either. Schindler, Richter and Mar's 2024 direct replication with narrative and expository texts is named in the sources and was not obtainable, so nothing is quoted from it.
misreadings: The original paper is read as showing that generating helps everything, and it does not. Experiment 3 found the benefit falling only on the produced word and not on the cue that constrained it, which is why Slamecka and Graf held that the name is accurate. Experiment 5 then failed to find that selectivity under cued recall, and they wrote that a conclusion should wait for a replication with more subjects. That replication is not cited here because none was located. The second error is running the two numbers together. Bertsch's .40 is a standardised difference and McCurdy's .102 is a raw difference in proportion of items remembered, so they are one finding in two currencies rather than two findings. The third error is treating effort as the explanation and reasoning that harder generation must help more. Bertsch and colleagues found incidental learning at .65 against intentional at .32, and tasks their coders rated hard at .46 against easy at .41, with overlapping intervals. Generating a whole target did beat generating part of it, .55 against .32, which is the one result that fits effort. The fourth is confusing this with the testing effect. Retrieval practice compares testing against restudying material already seen; generation compares producing an item against reading it, at the moment of first encounter. A design that restudies is not a design that generates. The last error is the one with practical cost. The word-level effect survives 310 experiments, and the attempt to move it onto textbook prose produced four reading advantages in seven experiments by the researchers whose own meta-analysis had reported g = 0.77 for that material.
